items.abstract: I present process models for motion on a graph Γ(V,E) along its edges, motivated by examples. I build random sequences of edges and I derive sequences of Fock states. Therefore, I can distinguish two kinds of process steps, acceptance and rejection, comparable to stimulated and spontaneous emission. There is always at least one vertex, which represents the vacuum of the system. Rejections and vacuum are not visible in a quantum grand canonical ensemble.
title: Random Walks Through Fock States of a Graph

items.abstract: <jats:p>Monolithic architectures are increasingly facing challenges due to growing data volumes and systems becoming more complex. As a result, organizations are moving towards modern architectures, such as microservices, which bring more scalable and modular options compared to the traditional monoliths. Decomposing monolithic applications into microservices involves a manual process of finding multiple functional units represented as service candidates, which is time consuming and costly, as it requires significant effort and expertise. Most existing decomposition approaches rely on traditional NLP techniques to capture semantic relationships between code elements. These techniques capture only low level semantics and fail to account for complex relationships and deep structural relationships among code entities in monolithic applications. To fill this gap, we propose MicroDec, an approach for identifying microservices within monolithic systems. MicroDec leverages static analysis to extract the classes of monolithic application and models the relationships as a graph. It captures contextual relationships between graph nodes using biased random walks and powerful large language models (LLMs). This combination of biased random walks and LLM-based embeddings enables the identification of service candidates with high cohesion and low coupling. We compare MicroDec with four state-of-the-art methods, using a large number of monolithic applications and evaluate the results with five metrics, which measure functional dependency and modularity of the proposed service candidates. Our results show that MicroDec outperforms the state-of-the-art methods across these key metrics.</jats:p>
title: MicroDec: Leveraging Graph-based Random Walks and Large Language Models for Microservice Decomposition

items.abstract: <jats:p>For network graphs, numerous graph features are intimately linked to eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix, such as connectivity and diameter. Thus, it is very important to solve eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix for graphs. Similarly, for higher-order networks, eigenvalues of combinatorial Laplacian matrices are also important for invariants of graphs. However, for large-scale networks, it is difficult to calculate eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix directly because it is either very difficult to obtain the whole network structure or requires a lot of computing resources. Therefore, this article makes the following contributions. Firstly, this paper proposes a random walk approach for estimating the bounds of the greatest eigenvalues of Laplacian matrices for large-scale networks. Considering the relationship between the spectral moments of the adjacency matrix and the closed paths in the network, we utilize the relationship between the adjacency matrix and the Laplacian matrix to establish the relationship between the Laplacian matrix and the closed paths. Then, we employ equiprobable random walks to sample the large graph to obtain the small graph. Through algebraic topology knowledge, we obtain the bounds of the largest eigenvalue of the Laplacian matrix of the large graph by using Laplacian spectral moments of the small graph. Secondly, for high-order networks, this paper proposes a method based on random walks and graph transformations. The graph transformation we propose mainly converts graphs with second-order simplices into ordinary weighted graphs, thereby transforming the problem of solving the spectral moments of the second-order combined Laplacian matrix into solving the spectral moments of the adjacency matrix. Then, we use the aforementioned random walk method to solve bounds of the greatest eigenvalue of the second-order combinatorial Laplacian matrix. Finally, by comparing the proposed method with existing algorithms in synthetic and real networks, its accuracy and superiority are demonstrated.</jats:p>
title: Estimate Laplacian Spectral Properties of Large-Scale Networks by Random Walks and Graph Transformation
